title: Onboarding Stability Sprint: Post-Go-Live Retro & Repair Sprint
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary
-------
This document defines the "Onboarding Stability Sprint": a focused 7–10 day cross-functional activity that runs immediately after an enterprise customer’s first live traffic cutover. The goal is to close early reliability gaps, stabilize cost/latency profiles, and deliver a structured retro that feeds QBR metrics and long-term remediation tickets.

Why this exists
----------------
Many go-lives appear successful on day-0 but surface repeated, low-severity reliability and cost issues over weeks (burst throttles, KV cache misses, cold-starts for rare routes). The Stability Sprint is a bounded, repeatable process to:
- Reduce mean time to remediation for non-critical but high-frequency issues
- Align engineering, SRE, product, and customer success on priority fixes
- Produce measurable outcomes for the customer’s first QBR and SLA review

Audience
--------
- Customer Success (primary owner)
- SRE and Runtime Engineering (operational remediation)
- Integrations and Solutions Engineering
- Product Manager for the customer
- Customer engineering contacts (participation as required)

Scope and success criteria
-------------------------
Inbound scope (what we cover during the sprint):
1) Stability: Reduce 95th/99th latency and error spikes for tenant routes observed in the first 72 hours
2) Cost alignment: Identify top 3 per-token cost drivers and produce short-term mitigations (batching changes, latency/cost routing)
3) Observability gaps: Add or refine telemetry assertions used for QBRs
4) Process: Triage and convert urgent fixes into tracked engineering work with owners and ETA

Success criteria (pass/fail):
- Pass: 3 of the 4 inbound scope goals completed and customer signs off on readiness for QBR metrics collection
- Partial: 1–2 goals completed with clear remediation plan and committed ship dates
- Fail: fewer than 1 goal completed and no committed remediation plan

Sprint cadence and timeline (example 7-day sprint)
-------------------------------------------------
Day 0 (cutover evening)
- Customer Success runs the cutover acceptance checklist and starts the sprint document
- SRE enables increased short-term telemetry retention for the tenant (72h high-fidelity window)

Day 1: Triage & quick wins
- Morning: 60–90 minute cross-functional triage meeting (see Meeting agenda below)
- Identify top 5 signals (errors, 99p latency routes, token-cost anomalies) and assign owners
- Implement 1–2 quick fixes (e.g., route pinning, temporary rate caps, client-side batching guidance)

Day 2–4: Focused repair work
- Parallel squads work queued tickets: instrumentation gaps, caching adjustments, configuration tuning
- Daily 30-minute sync for blockers and status updates

Day 5: Validation and hardening
- Run synthetic journeys (customer-specific) against fixed routes for 24–48h validation window
- Confirm telemetry assertions and cost telemetry alignment

Day 6–7: Retro and QBR prep
- Draft the sprint retro artifacts, remediation backlog, ownership matrix, and QBR-ready dashboard snapshots
- Customer Success coordinates a 60-minute stakeholder retro and produces a 1-page QBR summary

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Customer Success (CS): sprint owner; coordinates meetings, customer comms, and sign-off
- SRE Lead: owns incident-style triage and operational changes (routing, SLAs, infra tweaks)
- Runtime Eng: implements kernel/runtime/quantization configuration changes that affect latency/cost
- Integrations/SE: assists with client-side SDK guidance and validates contract changes
- Product: prioritizes cross-cutting product changes into roadmap if necessary

Triage meeting agenda (60–90 minutes)
------------------------------------
1) Quick status & customer impact summary (CS) — 5m
2) Top signals review (observability owner) — 10m
3) Action items and owners for quick fixes — 20m
4) Risk heatmap and decide if escalation to priority path required — 10m
5) Communication plan for customer (who says what and when) — 10m
6) Schedule re-checks and define success criteria — remaining time

Telemetry and synthetic checks (examples)
--------------------------------------
Key signals to monitor (minimum):
- 99th latency per route (ms)
- Error rate by tenant and route (5m/1h windows)
- KV cache miss ratio and effective hit amplification
- Per-request token cost variance (7d baseline comparison)
- Streaming connection resets & gRPC idle stream resets

Example telemetry assertion (JSON snippet used by the synthetic runner):
{
  "assertion_name": "tenant-99p-latency-under-400ms",
  "metric": "route.latency.99p",
  "tenant_id": "TENANT-1234",
  "threshold_ms": "400",
  "window_mins": "60"
}

Observability checklist (table)
------------------------------
| Item | Owner | Minimum requirement | Why it matters |
|------|-------|---------------------|----------------|
| 99p latency per-route | SRE | 5m resolution | Detect tail latency spikes |
| Token cost breakdown | Finance/CS | per-route / per-model | Surface cost drivers |
| KV cache hit rate | Runtime Eng | 1m resolution | Affects downstream latency & cost |
| Streaming resets | Integrations | 5m resolution | Client compatibility and stability |

Quick remediation patterns (common fixes)
-----------------------------------------
- Route-level pinning to a stable model variant for 24–72 hours
- Apply temporary soft rate-limits to bursty tenant endpoints (CS+SRE approved)
- Enable aggressive prefix caching for high-reuse prompt families
- Adjust batching window for low-latency interactive routes to reduce token churn
- Short-term increase in dedicated capacity (if contract allows) for traffic hot-paths

Escalation ladder for issues discovered during the sprint
------------------------------------------------------
1) Sprint triage owners (first responders) — 30m SLA for acknowledgement
2) SRE lead + Runtime Eng — 2h SLA to propose temporary mitigations
3) On-call manager / Eng Director — 4h SLA to approve emergency capacity or cross-region failover
4) Exec stakeholder & customer leadership — notify if >8h unresolved customer-impacting degradation

Communication templates (customer-facing)
----------------------------------------
Subject: Post-go-live stability sprint: initial findings
Hi <Customer Name> team,

Thank you again for your cutover last night. We’ve initiated a 7-day stability sprint to ensure the experience meets your SLAs. Initial observations: increased 99p latency on conversational route ‘chat/v1-consumer’, and an elevated token cost variance on the re-ranking route. We will: (1) pin the route to a stable model variant within 2 hours, (2) deploy a temporary rate cap on low-impact endpoints, and (3) share a daily 09:30 PST update for the next 72 hours.

If you prefer a different cadence or immediate technical deep-dive, please let us know.

Best,
Customer Success (Aisha Patel)

Retro template (to capture outcomes)
----------------------------------
- What went well (bullet list)
- What surprised us
- Highest impact fixes delivered (with ticket IDs)
- Outstanding risks and owners
- Recommended product/roadmap changes
- QBR metrics to include for next meeting

QBR integration and artifacts to produce
-------------------------------------
- 1-page sprint summary with: top-5 signals, fixes delivered, outstanding items, and customer sign-off
- QBR dashboard snapshot with: 99p latency trend, per-route cost, error-rate trend, synthetic journey pass-rate
- Remediation backlog grouped by priority and owner with ETA

Post-sprint handoff checklist
----------------------------
1) Ensure all temporary mitigations have explicit TTLs and owners (no open temporary configs)
2) Create corresponding tickets in the product/engineering backlog with linked JIRA IDs
3) Schedule follow-up check at 30 and 90 days post-cutover to validate long-term stability
4) Attach synthetic run artifacts and telemetry snapshots to the account record

Runbook snippets and commands
----------------------------
Example: temporarily pin a route to a model variant via the admin CLI:

bash
redwoodctl route update --tenant TENANT-1234 --route chat/v1-consumer --pin model:openlite-v2-quant --ttl 72h

Example: query 99p latency via metrics CLI (Prometheus-compatible):

bash
redwoodctl metrics query "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(route_request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant=\"TENANT-1234\"}[5m])) by (le, route))"

Appendix: typical remediation effort sizing
------------------------------------------
- Quick fixes: 1–4 engineer-hours (routing, config changes)
- Instrumentation gaps: 1–3 engineer-days (add metrics/assertions)
- Runtime changes requiring deploys: 3–10 engineer-days (may span releases)
- Product/roadmap work: tracked as epics (multi-sprint)

Appendix: decision log (example entries)
--------------------------------------
- 2026-11-05: Sprint framework ratified by CS and SRE leadership — A. Patel
- 2026-12-10: Added per-route cost telemetry requirement — M. Chen
- 2027-02-12: Expanded communication templates and telemetry assertions (Ravi Kumar)

Related documents and where to store artifacts
--------------------------------------------
- Store sprint artifacts (telemetry snapshots, synthetic runs) in the customer record folder: s3://redwood-enterprise-artifacts/<tenant-id>/stability-sprints/<date>/
- Link JIRA epics to the customer account in the CRM and include sprint summary PDF.

Notes and caveats
-----------------
- The Stability Sprint is not a replacement for emergency incident response. If a P0 occurs, follow the standard incident process and pause the sprint cadence in favor of incident postmortem flows.
- Customer opt-in: this sprint is part of our enterprise onboarding offering and should be presented as recommended but may be opted out by customers under special circumstances.
